title: Why Supabase, and what you are actually getting

blocks.text: This section answers the question you should ask before signing up for anything: what is Supabase, why does this course use it, and what does it cost you. By the end you will know where Supabase fits next to the other two ways this course lets you run SQL, what the free plan actually gives you, what it does not give you, and what to have ready before you start the sign-up in the next section.
What Supabase is, in plain terms

Supabase is a company that runs PostgreSQL databases for you. You create an account in a web browser, you create a project, and Supabase starts a real PostgreSQL database on its own servers. You then open `SQL Editor` in the left-hand sidebar of your project, type SQL into the editor, and click the `Run` button (or press `Ctrl+Enter` on Windows, `Cmd+Enter` on a Mac). Results appear in a panel below the editor. There is nothing to download, nothing to install, no server to start on your laptop, and no port numbers to type. For classwork it is free, and the Free plan does not ask for a credit card.

The word you will see everywhere in Supabase is `project`. For our purposes one project is one database, plus some extras this course does not need (an auto-generated web API, a login system, file storage). When the documentation says "your project," read it as "your database." Projects are grouped under an `organization`. Supabase creates a default organization for you automatically the first time you create an account, and assigns you the `Owner` role in it, so this is not something you have to set up.

blocks.label: PostgreSQL
blocks.text: PostgreSQL (often shortened to "Postgres") is a free, open-source relational database. It belongs to the same category of software as MySQL, Oracle Database, and Microsoft SQL Server -- they are all relational databases that speak SQL, though they are separate products from different vendors and only PostgreSQL and MySQL are open source. PostgreSQL stores tables, enforces primary and foreign keys, and speaks SQL -- everything Modules 1 and 2 describe applies to it without change.
Three places you can run SQL in this course
You now have three options, and they are good at different things. None of them replaces the others.

blocks.text: The in-page sandbox is deliberately throwaway. It is the fastest way to test whether a `SELECT` returns what you expected, and the safest place to make a mistake, but the moment you reload the page your tables are gone. A local install is permanent but it lives on exactly one machine: if you write your KimTay tables on a lab computer, they are not there when you get home, and a reformat takes them with it.

Supabase sits in between. The database is real, it keeps your data, and you reach it from any computer that has a web browser -- you sign in to the Supabase dashboard with your Supabase account (your sign-up email and password, or your GitHub login). If your laptop dies the week before an assignment is due, your `REP` and `CUSTOMER` tables are still sitting on Supabase's server exactly as you left them, and you can open them from a lab machine or a library computer.
One honest catch: it is Postgres, not MySQL

Module 3 teaches MySQL-flavoured SQL. Supabase gives you PostgreSQL. The great majority of what you have learned transfers untouched -- `CREATE TABLE`, `PRIMARY KEY`, `FOREIGN KEY`, `NOT NULL`, `INSERT INTO`, `SELECT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`, and the `VARCHAR`, `CHAR`, `DECIMAL`, `SMALLINT`, and `DATE` types all exist in PostgreSQL and behave the same way for everything this course asks you to do. A small number of things differ. You will not use `CREATE DATABASE`: PostgreSQL does have that statement, but your project already is the database, and the statement will fail in the SQL Editor anyway because the editor wraps what you run in a transaction and PostgreSQL forbids `CREATE DATABASE` inside one. `DESCRIBE` is a MySQL command that PostgreSQL does not have at all. And PostgreSQL quietly lowercases unquoted table and column names, so `CREATE TABLE REP` actually creates a table named `rep` -- harmless as long as you never wrap a name in double quotes, which is why this course does not.

blocks.label: Where the differences are listed
blocks.text: Do not try to memorize the differences now. Section S-6 puts the MySQL statement and the PostgreSQL statement side by side for every case Module 3 uses, including the full KimTay DDL rewritten for Postgres and the replacement for `DESCRIBE`. Work through the setup first, then use S-6 as your reference sheet.
What the free plan gives you
The Supabase Free plan is genuinely free, needs no credit card, and is more than enough for this course. Three limits are worth knowing before you start.

blocks.caption: Free plan limits that matter for this course
rows: 2 active projects

Your account can have two free projects running at the same time. This is a total across every organization where you are an Owner or Administrator -- it is not two per organization. Paused projects do not count against it, so plan on one project for KimTay and keep the second slot free.
500 MB database size per project
Each project gets its own half gigabyte of database storage. The whole KimTay database is a few kilobytes, so you will not come close.
Paused after 1 week of inactivity

If a free project goes seven days without database activity, Supabase pauses it to save resources. Supabase emails the project owner a warning roughly a week beforehand, and again once the project has actually been paused.

blocks.label: Pausing is not deletion
blocks.text: A paused project stops serving requests, but your tables, rows, and settings are all preserved on disk. To bring it back, open the Supabase dashboard, click your organization, click the paused project, then click `Resume project` and confirm. Restoring takes a few minutes. You have a one-year window to restore a paused project from the dashboard; after that the backups have expired and it may not be recoverable. What counts as "activity" is requests to the database, not merely loading the dashboard -- so to keep a project awake, actually run a statement in the SQL Editor (`select 1;` is enough) once or twice a week.

blocks.label: The Free plan does not back up your data
blocks.text: Automatic daily backups are a paid-plan feature; Free plan projects have none. Supabase keeping your database running is not the same as Supabase keeping a copy of it. Before you submit any assignment, save your own copy of the SQL that builds and fills your tables -- keep the `CREATE TABLE` and `INSERT` statements in a text file on your computer or in cloud storage. If anything ever goes wrong, you can rebuild the whole KimTay database by pasting that file back into the SQL Editor.
One security label you will see, and why it is fine here

blocks.label: "Unrestricted" is expected for coursework
blocks.text: Tables you create by typing `CREATE TABLE` in the SQL Editor do not have PostgreSQL's Row Level Security turned on, and the Table Editor will show them with a red `Unrestricted` label. For this course that label is expected and is not an error -- it simply means the database is not filtering rows per end user, which is exactly what you want while doing KimTay exercises. Supabase also stopped exposing new `public` tables to a project's auto-generated Data API by default for projects created after 30 May 2026, so a project you create today is not publishing your coursework to the internet. Two rules anyway: do not put real personal data in a course project, and if you ever reuse this project for a public application, read Supabase's Row Level Security guide first.
Two different passwords -- do not mix them up

The sign-up in S-2 involves two separate passwords, and confusing them is the most common way students get stuck. Your **account password** is what you type at the Supabase sign-in page to reach the dashboard; if you sign up with GitHub instead, your GitHub login plays this role and there is no Supabase account password. Your **database password** is a different string, created when you create the project, and the SQL Editor never asks for it -- you only need it for a desktop client such as pgAdmin or `psql` (section S-5, optional) and for connection strings.

Supabase does not display the database password again after the project is created, so write it down when you create it. If you do lose it, you are not locked out of anything: you can set a new database password from the project's Database settings page in the dashboard, and your account login is unaffected either way.
What you need before the next section
Sign-up is mostly filling in a short form; Supabase then takes a few minutes to build your database before the SQL Editor will run anything. Budget about fifteen minutes and have these ready.

items: An email address you can open right now -- Supabase sends a confirmation link you must click before you can sign in. (Signing up with a GitHub account also works and skips the password step; there is no Google option.)
A web browser: Chrome, Edge, Safari, or Firefox, all fine
A name for your project (`kimtay` is a good choice) and a region -- you will be asked for both, and picking the region geographically closest to you keeps queries fast

Somewhere to write down the database password the project-creation form asks you to set -- a password manager, a notes app, or paper. Supabase will not show it to you again, though you can reset it later if you lose it.
About 15 minutes, including a few minutes of waiting while the project is created
No credit card. The Free plan does not ask for payment details.
Nothing installed. If you want a desktop tool such as pgAdmin or `psql` later, section S-5 covers it, and it is optional.

blocks.text: How you will know it worked

You are done with setup when you can do this, at the end of section S-2: open your project, click `SQL Editor` in the left-hand sidebar, type `select version();`, and click `Run`. Within a second or two a results panel appears below the editor showing one row in one column, and the text in it begins with the word `PostgreSQL` followed by a version number. That single line proves three things at once -- your account works, the project finished building, and you are talking to a real PostgreSQL database. If instead you see a spinner that never resolves, or a message that the project is still being set up, wait a minute and click `Run` again; the database is usually still provisioning.
When you have those, continue to section S-2 and create your account.

title: Create your Supabase project

blocks.text: By the end of this section you will have a real PostgreSQL database running on the internet, owned by you, that you can reach from a browser in about ten minutes and without installing anything. Nothing here costs money -- Supabase's Free plan does not ask for a credit card. You will not create any tables yet; the goal is an empty, healthy database and a saved password. Read step 6 carefully, because it is the one step students skip and the only one that is genuinely painful to undo.

blocks.label: Before you start
blocks.text: You need three things: a web browser, an email address you can check right now, and about ten minutes. You do not need to install anything, you do not need to open a terminal, and you do not need a credit card. If you already have a GitHub account, signing in with it saves a step. Before you begin, open a second window with your password manager (1Password, Bitwarden, Apple Passwords, your browser's built-in one) or, if you have none, your computer's notes app -- step 6 asks you to save something the instant it appears, and you do not want to be hunting for a place to put it.

items.title: Create your Supabase account
items.body: Go to `https://supabase.com/dashboard/sign-up`. You have two options. Click `Continue with GitHub` and authorize Supabase -- fastest if you already have a GitHub account. Or type an email address and a password into the form and submit it; Supabase then emails you a confirmation link, and the account is not active until you click it. Use an email you actually check, and if the message has not arrived in a couple of minutes look in your spam or junk folder. The account password must be at least 8 characters with an uppercase letter, a lowercase letter, a number, and a special character. Important: this password logs you in to the Supabase website. It is **not** the database password you create in step 6. They are two different secrets and you will end up needing both.

items.title: Land in an organization
items.body: An organization is the container that holds your projects, and later your billing and any teammates. New accounts normally get one created automatically with you as the Owner, so there is usually nothing to do here. If instead Supabase shows you a form asking you to create one, fill it in: any name works (`keiser-db` or your own name is fine) and choose the **Free** plan when asked. One organization is all this course needs.

items.title: Start a new project
items.body: From your organization's `Projects` page, click the `New project` button. If your dashboard is empty and you cannot find the button, go straight to `https://supabase.com/dashboard/new/_` -- the `_` on the end tells Supabase to use whichever organization you were last in. Either way you land on a page headed `Create a new project`.

items.title: Check the `Organization` field
items.body: The first field on the form is `Organization`. If you only have one, it is already filled in and you can move on. If you somehow have more than one, pick the free organization from step 2 -- creating the project under the wrong organization is the kind of mistake that turns into a surprise bill later.

items.title: Name the project
items.body: In the `Project name` field, type something you will still recognize in three weeks. `kimtay` is a good choice, since KimTay Pet Supplies is the database you are about to build. This name is only a label in the dashboard -- it does not become the name of the database (that is always `postgres`), and you can rename it later under `Project Settings` then `General`.

items.title: Generate the database password, then save it before you touch anything else
items.body: Find the field labelled `Database password`. Directly beneath it is a password-strength meter with a small `Generate a password` link -- click that link. Supabase fills the field with a long random password, shown as dots because it is a password field, and a copy icon appears at the right-hand edge of the field. Click the copy icon, then immediately paste the password into your password manager or notes app. Give the entry a name like "Supabase kimtay DATABASE password" so you can tell it apart from your supabase.com login. Do not paste it into a file inside a project folder you will push to GitHub, and do not plan to retype it from memory. Do not click away from this form until it is saved somewhere -- the moment you create the project, the dashboard's own Database settings page will tell you that "the database password isn't viewable after creation."

items.title: Choose the region closest to you
items.body: Open the `Region` dropdown. The top group is labelled `General regions` and holds a few broad choices; below it is a longer list of specific AWS data centers, city by city. Students in Florida should pick `East US (North Virginia)`, which appears in both groups -- either entry is fine. The rest of the list is for people in other parts of the world. Pick the location physically nearest to where you sit.

items.title: Leave the `Security` options at their defaults
items.body: Below the region is a `Security` block with checkboxes such as `Enable Data API`, `Automatically expose new tables`, and `Enable automatic RLS`. Accept whatever Supabase has pre-selected. This course drives the database from the SQL Editor and from desktop tools that connect as the `postgres` user, and none of these settings affect either path, so there is nothing to change and nothing you can break here. If you also see options named `High availability` or `Compute size`, leave them off or at the smallest default -- those are paid add-ons.

items.title: Click `Create new project` and wait
items.body: Press the `Create new project` button at the bottom of the form. The dashboard opens immediately and shows the project in a setting-up state. Leave the tab open and give it a minute or two -- see "What the wait is" below.

blocks.text: Why the password step is the one that bites people

That generated password is the credential every outside tool uses to connect directly to your database -- `psql`, pgAdmin, TablePlus, or an application you write later. Specifically, it is the password for the Postgres user named `postgres`. Supabase does not keep a readable copy of it: Postgres stores only a hash, so there is nothing for the dashboard to show you. The dashboard says so itself, in plain words, on the page where you would go looking: "The database password isn't viewable after creation." There is no reveal button anywhere.

blocks.label: Shown once, never shown again
blocks.text: If you lose the database password you cannot recover it -- you can only reset it. The reset lives in the left sidebar under `Database`, then `Settings`, in the `Database password` section (`Reset database password`). A reset is not the end of the world, but the new password invalidates every connection string you have already saved in a tool or a script, so you will be re-pasting it in several places. Save it the first time. And keep it clearly labelled: this is a different password from the one you use to sign in to supabase.com, and resetting the wrong one does not help.
What the region choice actually affects

The region is the physical data center where your Postgres server lives. It affects one thing you will notice: round-trip time. Every query you run travels from your laptop to that data center and back, so a database in Virginia answers a student in Florida in a few dozen milliseconds, while one in Sydney adds a visible pause -- closer to a quarter of a second -- to every single statement. It does not change the SQL, the data types, the price, or the Free-plan limits.

"Closest to you" is the right default for coursework because you are the only user. In a real product you would pick the region closest to your users instead, which is not always where you are. Pick carefully now: a project is bound to its region at the hardware level on every plan, not just the free one. Supabase's own guidance is that the only way to change region is to create a new project in the region you want and migrate the data across -- so for coursework, a wrong choice means building the schema again.
What the wait is

Supabase is provisioning a dedicated Postgres instance for you, creating the default database (it is called `postgres`), and starting the API, authentication, and storage services that sit in front of it. The dashboard's own wording is that your project will be ready in a few minutes; in practice it is usually one to three. You do not need to reload the page -- the status updates itself, moving from a setting-up state through `Starting` to an active project. If you open the `SQL Editor` too early and a query fails with a connection error, wait thirty seconds and run it again rather than assuming something is broken.
Confirm it worked

Once the setup banner clears, click `SQL Editor` in the left sidebar. A blank query tab normally opens by itself. If the editor is showing something else instead, click the small `+` button at the top of the SQL Editor's snippet list -- hovering it shows the tooltip `Create a new query` -- and choose `Create a new snippet`. Type or paste the statement below into the editor, then press the `Run` button, or use `Cmd+Enter` on a Mac and `Ctrl+Enter` on Windows.
SELECT version();

`version()` is a built-in PostgreSQL function that reports the server's version string, and this is about the smallest valid statement that proves a database is answering you. You should get a results grid with exactly one row and one column named `version`, whose value begins with the word `PostgreSQL` followed by a version number and some build details. The details do not matter; any output at all means your database is alive and you are talking to it. If you instead get a red error about the connection or about the project not being ready, the project is still starting -- wait half a minute and press `Run` again.

items: The project appears in your dashboard in an active state -- not `Paused`, not `Starting`, not still setting up.
The left sidebar shows `Table Editor`, `SQL Editor`, `Database`, `Authentication`, and `Storage` (there are more items below those, which is normal).
`SELECT version();` in the SQL Editor returns one row, in a column named `version`, whose value starts with `PostgreSQL`.
`Table Editor` opens on the `public` schema and offers to create your first table. An empty table list is the correct result here -- you have not created any yet.

Your database password is saved outside any folder you push to GitHub, somewhere you can find it in a week, and labelled clearly enough that you will know it is the *database* password and not your supabase.com login.
You can get back to everything above by visiting `https://supabase.com/dashboard` and signing in. Nothing you just built lives only on this computer.

blocks.label: Never commit the database password or a secret API key
blocks.text: Two kinds of secret belong to this project. The first is the database password you just saved. The second is your project's **secret API key**, a string beginning `sb_secret_`, which you will meet later under `Project Settings` then `API Keys` (it is also surfaced in the project's `Connect` dialog). Older tutorials call this the `service_role` key; Supabase stopped issuing `service_role` and `anon` keys to newly created projects in November 2025, so on a project you create today the `sb_secret_` key is the equivalent, and the safe-to-share public one is `sb_publishable_`. Both the database password and the secret key grant full control of the database and both bypass every Row Level Security rule. Do not paste either into a file you commit to GitHub, a shared Google Doc, a Discord or group chat, a screenshot, or a homework submission. Bots scan public repositories for exactly these strings within minutes of a push. If you ever suspect one leaked: reset the database password at `Database` then `Settings`, and delete and recreate the secret key at `Project Settings` then `API Keys`.

blocks.label: Free-plan facts worth knowing now
blocks.text: The Free plan gives you up to 2 free projects across all of your organizations, with 500 MB of database storage each -- far more than the KimTay data will ever need -- and it does not require a credit card. Supabase pauses Free-plan projects that show low activity over a 7-day window, and what it measures is real database activity, not whether you looked at the dashboard: its own guidance is that a few user requests to the database per day is enough to keep a project awake. So the reliable habit between class sessions is to open the `SQL Editor` and actually run something, even just `SELECT 1;`. Supabase does email the project owner a warning roughly a week before a pause takes effect, and after that warning arrives, simply opening the project in the dashboard is enough to stop it. A paused project keeps all of your data: select it in the dashboard, click `Resume project`, and it is back in about a minute. You have up to a year to resume a paused project, so a pause costs you a few minutes, not your work.

## Factual errors found and fixed (all verified against supabase.com/docs, supabase.com/pricing, and the live `supabase/supabase` Studio source, which is the authoritative record of the dashboard's own UI strings)

**1. `service_role` key no longer exists on new projects (most serious error).**
The original security callout told students they "will see [the `service_role` key] later under the `Connect` panel." Per Supabase's API-keys migration timeline (discussion #29260), *"New projects no longer have `anon` and `service_role` available for use"* as of **November 2025**. A project created today gets `sb_publishable_...` / `sb_secret_...` keys instead. Legacy keys are slated for deletion "Late 2026, TBC." Rewrote the callout around `sb_secret_`, noted the `service_role` synonym so students can read older tutorials, and added `sb_publishable_` as the safe-to-share counterpart.

**2. API keys are not primarily in the "Connect" panel.**
Official location is `Settings > API Keys` (route `/project/[ref]/settings/api-keys` confirmed in the repo tree); the Connect dialog also surfaces them. Corrected to name both, primary first.

**3. Project pausing claim was wrong.**
Original: *"opening the dashboard or running a query counts as activity, so visiting once during the week keeps it awake."* The official `free-project-pausing` doc says pausing is judged on **user database activity** — *"Typically a few user requests to the database each day over the previous week is enough"* — and dashboard-visiting is listed only as a remedy **after the warning email arrives**, not as general week-to-week activity. Rewrote accordingly, and added the two facts the original omitted: the warning email, and the **1-year restore window**.

**4. Field label is `Database password`, not `Database Password`.**
Confirmed in `ProjectCreation/DatabasePasswordInput.tsx` (`label="Database password"`). `Project name`, `Region`, `Organization`, and the `Generate a password` link text (in `PasswordStrengthBar.tsx`) all check out as written.

**5. "The three fields on the New project form" is out of date.**

title: Run your first SQL in the Supabase SQL Editor

blocks.text: This is the section where the account you made starts paying off. In the next ten minutes you will open Supabase's SQL Editor, prove your connection works with a one-line query, then build the KimTay `REP` table and load the three reps -- the same table you built in Module 3, except this time the rows live on a real Postgres server and are still there tomorrow. Everything happens in your browser. You will not open a terminal, install anything, or type a password at a command prompt.

blocks.label: Before you start
blocks.text: You need the free Supabase account and the project you created in the previous section, and you need to be signed in. If you just created the project, look at its status on the dashboard first -- a brand-new project spends a minute or two setting up, and SQL run against it before it is ready will fail with a connection error rather than a SQL error. Wait until the project opens normally and stops saying it is being set up.
Open the SQL Editor and prove the connection works

items.title: Open your project
items.body: Go to `supabase.com/dashboard` and click the project you created. If you belong to more than one organization, pick the organization first, then the project. You land on the project dashboard, with a narrow icon sidebar down the left edge. **How you know it worked:** the project name appears at the top of the page and the sidebar is visible.

items.title: Click SQL Editor
items.body: In the left sidebar, click `SQL Editor`. On a narrow window the sidebar collapses to icons only -- hover over each icon and the name appears in a tooltip; `SQL Editor` is the one shaped like a small terminal window. If you are already signed in, the address `supabase.com/dashboard/project/_/sql/new` also works: the `_` is a placeholder that Supabase swaps for whichever project you used last, so check the project name at the top before you run anything.

items.title: Start a new query
items.body: Click `New query`. You get an empty text area on top and an empty results panel underneath. This is where every statement in this section goes. **How you know it worked:** there is a tab or entry named `Untitled query`, and the text area is empty and accepts typing.

items.title: Run one line
items.body: Click inside the text area, type the statement below, then click the green `Run` button (or press `Cmd+Enter` on a Mac, `Ctrl+Enter` on Windows or Linux). The results panel replaces its empty state with a small table.

blocks.text: SELECT version();

The results panel shows one row with one column, headed `version`, holding a long line of text that begins with the word `PostgreSQL` followed by a version number. The line is wider than the panel, so you may have to scroll the results sideways to read all of it -- you do not need to. Seeing `PostgreSQL` at the front is your proof: your browser reached a real Postgres server, the server ran your SQL, and it sent an answer back. Nothing was installed on your computer to make that happen.

blocks.label: If you see a red error instead
blocks.text: An error that mentions the project being paused means Supabase put a Free plan project to sleep, which it does after roughly a week of very little activity. Go back to `supabase.com/dashboard`, click the project, click `Resume project`, and confirm. Give it a minute or two, then run `SELECT version();` again. If instead you get a network or connection error on a brand-new project, it is still finishing setup -- wait a minute and retry. A red error that quotes your own SQL back at you is a different thing entirely: that is a typo, and the message names the line and position to look at.
Build the REP table

Clear the editor first: click anywhere inside the text area, press `Cmd+A` on a Mac or `Ctrl+A` on Windows or Linux to select everything, then press Delete. Now paste the `CREATE TABLE` below. This is the exact KimTay `REP` definition from Module 3. Postgres accepts `CHAR`, `VARCHAR`, and `DECIMAL` with the same meanings you learned there, so nothing has to change -- with one difference worth knowing: Postgres actually enforces the sizes. The browser sandbox lets a 40-character name sit happily in a `VARCHAR(15)`; Postgres rejects it with a `value too long` error. That is the stricter, more realistic behavior, and it is one of the reasons to move here.

CREATE TABLE REP (
    REP_NUM      CHAR(2)      PRIMARY KEY,
    LAST_NAME    VARCHAR(15)  NOT NULL,
    FIRST_NAME   VARCHAR(15)  NOT NULL,
    STREET       VARCHAR(20),
    CITY         VARCHAR(15),
    STATE        CHAR(2),
    ZIP          CHAR(5),
    COMMISSION   DECIMAL(8,2),
    RATE         DECIMAL(4,2)
);

Click `Run`. A successful `CREATE TABLE` returns no rows, so the results panel says `Success. No rows returned`. That is what you want -- it is not an empty result that failed quietly, it is the normal response to a statement that changes the database rather than asking it a question. The table now exists on the server, and it will still exist after you close the browser.

blocks.label: Why the table shows up as lowercase rep
blocks.text: Postgres folds unquoted names to lower case, so `REP` is stored as `rep` and `REP_NUM` as `rep_num`. You can keep writing your SQL in upper case exactly as the course does -- Postgres folds your query the same way, so it still matches. The only rule to remember is not to wrap a name in double quotes unless you are willing to type those quotes every time afterwards: `CREATE TABLE "REP"` really does create a table whose name is upper case, and from then on `SELECT * FROM REP;` will fail with `relation "rep" does not exist`.

blocks.label: How to start over if you run something twice
blocks.text: Unlike the sandbox on this page, this database remembers. Running the `CREATE TABLE` a second time fails with `relation "rep" already exists`, and running the inserts twice fails with `duplicate key value violates unique constraint "rep_pkey"` -- both are the server correctly refusing to duplicate work, not a broken setup. To wipe the slate and rebuild, run `DROP TABLE IF EXISTS REP;` and then run the `CREATE TABLE` and the inserts again. Supabase shows a confirmation dialog before it runs a destructive statement such as `DROP` or `DELETE`; read it, then confirm.
Insert the three reps

Clear the editor again (`Cmd+A` or `Ctrl+A`, then Delete) and paste all three `INSERT` statements. Notice each one ends with a semicolon -- that is how the editor knows where one statement stops and the next begins. All three go in one run.
Run it. You get `Success. No rows returned` again -- inserts change the database, they do not answer a question, so there is nothing to show. Now ask for the data back:
SELECT * FROM REP ORDER BY REP_NUM;

Three rows: Kaiser, Hull, Perez. The `ORDER BY` is there on purpose -- a plain `SELECT * FROM REP;` also returns all three, but no database promises you a particular order unless you ask for one, so do not read anything into the order you happen to get. Same result as the sandbox on this page, with one difference that matters: close this tab, come back next week, run it again, and the three rows are still there.

blocks.label: Run only part of your script
blocks.text: If you highlight some text before clicking `Run` (or pressing `Cmd+Enter` / `Ctrl+Enter`), the editor runs only the highlighted statements and ignores the rest. That is the fastest way to work through a long script: keep every statement in one query and highlight just the line you want to test. If nothing is highlighted, everything in the editor runs, top to bottom -- which is also the usual reason a `DROP` you thought was safely parked at the bottom of the file suddenly runs.

blocks.caption: The sandbox on this page vs. the Supabase SQL Editor
rows: Engine
SQLite, running inside your browser
PostgreSQL, running on a server

Gone when you reload the page
Kept until you delete it
Column sizes
`VARCHAR(15)` is not enforced
`VARCHAR(15)` is enforced; oversized values are rejected

blocks.text: Name the query so you can find it again

Supabase already saved this query for you -- every query you run in the SQL Editor is kept as a snippet in your project, which is why the left-hand list is filling up with entries called `Untitled query`. The part you have to do is give it a name. Click the query's name above the editor, or open the `...` menu next to its entry in the left-hand list and choose the rename option, and call it `KimTay - create REP`. Clicking a snippet in that list loads it back into the editor. This is the Supabase version of the habit Module 3 taught you with saved `.sql` script files: write it once, keep it, run it again when you need to rebuild. Snippets live in your Supabase account, not in the database, so they are not part of your data and will not appear in a backup of your tables -- keep a copy of anything you cannot afford to lose.
The point-and-click alternative: Table Editor

You do not have to use SQL to make a table here. Click `Table Editor` in the left sidebar, then `New table`, give it a name, click `Save`, and add columns one at a time with `New column` -- pick a name and a data type, then `Save`. Your `rep` table is already in that list; if you do not see it, reload the page, because the Table Editor caches the table list and does not always notice a table created in another tab. The Table Editor is a reasonable way to look at data you already have, and clicking through a table's rows is easier than typing a `SELECT` every time. It is a poor way to learn, though, because the design decisions you made in Module 2 get buried in a form instead of written down in a script you can save, read, and hand to someone else. Build with SQL, browse with the Table Editor.

blocks.label: Two separate switches control who can reach a table from outside the dashboard
blocks.text: The first is Row Level Security, or RLS, which decides which rows a request is allowed to see. The `New table` form in the Table Editor has an `Enable Row Level Security (RLS)` box that is ticked by default, and a table with RLS on and no policies returns zero rows to any app connecting with your project's publishable key (the `anon` key on older projects) -- while the Table Editor still shows every row, because the dashboard connects as an administrator. That mismatch is the single most common "my app is broken" moment in Supabase, and the app is behaving exactly as configured. A table you create with SQL, like the `REP` table you just built, starts with RLS off, and Supabase marks it in the dashboard with an `Unrestricted` badge and an `RLS disabled in public` warning. The second switch is Postgres grants, which decide whether a role may touch the table at all, and this default changed during 2026: projects created before May 30, 2026 automatically granted select, insert, update, and delete on every new table in the `public` schema to the `anon`, `authenticated`, and `service_role` roles, so an RLS-off table genuinely was readable by anything holding the publishable key. Projects created on or after May 30, 2026 do not do that -- a new table in `public` is invisible to the Data API until you write an explicit `GRANT` -- and Supabase applies the same setting to all remaining older projects on October 30, 2026. None of this changes anything you did in this section, because the SQL Editor talks to the database directly with administrator privileges. It matters the moment you point an application at the database. Before you put real data in any table in the `public` schema, run `ALTER TABLE REP ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;` and write at least one policy, then grant only the access each role actually needs.

items: `SELECT version();` returns one row in a column headed `version`, starting with the word `PostgreSQL`
`CREATE TABLE REP (...)` reports `Success. No rows returned`
The three `INSERT` statements run with no errors
`SELECT * FROM REP ORDER BY REP_NUM;` returns exactly three rows: Kaiser, Hull, Perez
You can recover from a mistake: `DROP TABLE IF EXISTS REP;` followed by the create and the inserts rebuilds the table from scratch
Your query is renamed from `Untitled query` and you can find it again in the SQL Editor's left-hand list
`rep` appears in the Table Editor's table list, and you can explain why it is lowercase
You can explain why the SQL Editor shows you rows that an app using the publishable key might not see

title: Connect from your own machine: Mac

blocks.text: So far you have run SQL inside a browser tab. This section gets your Mac talking to your Supabase database directly, using a real SQL client that you own. The payoff is that you can open a saved script, run it against your own KimTay tables, and see results without the Supabase dashboard in the way. You will do two things: copy one connection string, then hand that string to a client. Pick either the point-and-click route (a GUI app) or the terminal route. You do not need both.

blocks.label: Before you start
blocks.text: You need three things: (1) the Supabase project you created earlier in this course, with your KimTay tables already loaded; (2) the database password you set when you created that project, or the willingness to reset it -- resetting is safe and takes about a minute; (3) about 15 minutes. Nothing here costs money. If you are on the terminal route, you also need macOS 14 (Sonoma) or newer, which is what Homebrew supports today.
Step 1: copy the connection string

A connection string is one line of text that tells a client where the database lives and who you are. Supabase generates it for you. You never type it from memory, and you never copy one out of a tutorial -- every project has its own.

items.title: Open your project
items.body: Go to `supabase.com/dashboard` and click the project you created for this course.

items.title: Click Connect
items.body: The `Connect` button sits at the top of the project dashboard and opens a panel. This is where connection strings now live. Older tutorials send you to `Project Settings` then `Database` for the connection string -- that is out of date.

items.title: Find the connection-string list
items.body: The panel has several tabs for different tools (app frameworks, ORMs, and so on). You want the plain connection strings. In that list you will see three entries: `Direct connection`, `Transaction pooler`, and `Session pooler`. Click the copy icon next to `Session pooler`.

items.title: Paste it somewhere safe
items.body: Paste it into a plain text file for a moment. It looks like `postgresql://postgres.abcdefghijklmnopqrst:[YOUR-PASSWORD]@aws-1-us-east-1.pooler.supabase.com:5432/postgres`. Two parts of that are yours alone: `abcdefghijklmnopqrst` is your project reference, and the host name encodes your project's region. The `[YOUR-PASSWORD]` part is a placeholder -- replace it, square brackets and all, with the database password you set when you created the project.

blocks.label: Do not copy the example host
blocks.text: The host in the example above is an example. Yours will differ in both the region (`us-east-1`, `eu-central-1`, `ap-southeast-2`, ...) and the number after `aws-` -- Supabase issues `aws-0-`, `aws-1-`, and others, and there is no way to guess which one your project got. Always paste the host from your own `Connect` panel. Copying a host from a tutorial is the single most common reason a connection never resolves.

blocks.label: Why the session pooler
blocks.text: On a free project the direct connection resolves to an IPv6 address only, unless you buy the IPv4 add-on. Most home and campus networks are IPv4 only, so a direct connection on port `5432` will sit there and eventually time out with no useful message. Both pooler endpoints are reachable over IPv4 on every plan. Session mode behaves like a normal, long-lived Postgres connection and supports prepared statements, which is exactly what a desktop client wants.

blocks.caption: Which connection to pick for this course
rows: Direct connection
`db.[PROJECT-REF].supabase.co`
Servers on IPv6, some backup tools. Not your laptop on a typical network.
Session pooler
`aws-N-[REGION].pooler.supabase.com`
psql, TablePlus, pgAdmin 4. This is your choice.
Transaction pooler
`aws-N-[REGION].pooler.supabase.com`
Serverless and edge functions. Does not support prepared statements. Not this course.

blocks.label: Forgot the password
blocks.text: The database password is shown only while you are creating the project, and Supabase cannot show it to you again. If you did not save it, do not guess -- reset it. In the dashboard's left sidebar click `Database`, then `Settings` (the page URL ends in `/database/settings`), and use the reset-password control there. Set the new password, then go back to `Connect` and copy the string again. Resetting does not touch your tables or data.
Step 2 (route A): connect with a GUI client
A GUI client gives you a window with your tables on the left and a query editor on the right. Two are worth your time on a Mac. Pick one -- installing both just doubles the setup.

cards.title: TablePlus
cards.body: Download from `tableplus.com/download`. It is fast, quiet, and the easiest of the two to learn. It is paid software, but the trial never expires; it limits you to `2` open tabs and `2` open windows at a time, which is plenty for this course. Requires macOS 10.13 or newer and runs on both Intel and Apple Silicon from a single download. Best pick if your Mac is older.

cards.title: pgAdmin 4
cards.body: Download from `pgadmin.org/download/pgadmin-4-macos`. It is free and open source, built by the PostgreSQL community, with no usage limits. The interface is busier and it runs inside a browser-like window, so expect more clicking. There are separate Intel and Apple Silicon downloads -- pick the one matching your Mac (Apple menu, `About This Mac`, look at `Chip` or `Processor`). Current releases require macOS 13 (Ventura) or newer.

blocks.text: Both apps ask for the same five pieces of information, and all five are sitting inside the connection string you copied. Read the string left to right: after `postgresql://` (Supabase sometimes writes `postgres://` -- same thing) comes the user, then the first `:` and the password, then `@` and the host, then the last `:` and the port, then `/` and the database name.

blocks.caption: Filling in a new connection from your string
rows: Host
Everything between `@` and the last `:`

blocks.label: Keep the dot in the user name
blocks.text: On the session pooler the user name is `postgres`, then a dot, then your project reference -- for example `postgres.abcdefghijklmnopqrst`. Students often shorten it to plain `postgres` and get the error `Tenant or user not found`. Copy the whole thing, dot included.

In TablePlus: click `Create a new connection...`, choose `PostgreSQL`, give it a name like `KimTay`, fill the five fields, click `Test` (the fields turn green when they are reachable), then `Connect`. If TablePlus offers an `SSL mode` option, `PREFERRED` works and `REQUIRED` is stricter; either connects.

In pgAdmin 4: right-click `Servers` in the left tree, choose `Register` then `Server...`. On the `General` tab put any nickname you like in `Name`. On the `Connection` tab, note that pgAdmin uses slightly different labels -- `Host name/address`, `Port`, `Maintenance database` (this is the `Database` field: enter `postgres`), `Username`, and `Password`. Tick `Save password?` so you do not retype it. pgAdmin defaults to an SSL mode of `prefer`, which already encrypts the connection to Supabase; if you want to force it, go to the `Parameters` tab, click `+`, choose `SSL mode`, and set it to `require`.

blocks.label: How to know the GUI worked
blocks.text: You should see your KimTay tables, not just a connected server. In TablePlus the left sidebar lists them under the `public` schema. In pgAdmin, expand the server, then `Databases`, then `postgres`, then `Schemas`, then `public`, then `Tables` -- your course tables are there. If you connect but see no tables, you are connected to the right server but looking at the wrong schema; make sure you are under `public`, not `auth` or `storage`. Right-click a table and choose the view/preview option to confirm rows come back.
Step 3 (route B, optional): the terminal route with psql

`psql` is the official PostgreSQL command-line client. It is the fastest way to run a saved `.sql` script against your database, and it is what you will see in most documentation. macOS does not ship it, so you install it. Skip this whole step if the GUI is working for you -- nothing later in the course requires it.

blocks.label: If you have never used Terminal
blocks.text: Terminal is an app where you type one command, press `Return`, and read the text it prints back. Open it with `Command` + `Space`, type `Terminal`, press `Return`. Paste with `Command` + `V` like anywhere else. Commands below are one per line unless shown together -- press `Return` after each. Nothing here can damage your Mac, and you can close the window at any time.
First check whether you already have psql. Run:
psql --version

If that prints something like `psql (PostgreSQL) 17.6`, skip ahead to the connect command. If it prints `zsh: command not found: psql`, continue. Next, check for Homebrew, the package manager most Mac developers use to install command-line tools:
brew --version

If that prints a version, skip to installing `libpq`. If it prints `command not found`, install Homebrew with the official one-line installer below. It will ask for your Mac login password (nothing appears on screen while you type it -- that is normal), it may first install Apple's Command Line Tools, which is a large download, and the whole thing can take five to fifteen minutes and print a lot of output.
/bin/bash -c "$(curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Homebrew/install/HEAD/install.sh)"

When it finishes, read the last few lines. Homebrew prints a `Next steps:` section containing two lines it wants you to run, and those lines already contain the correct path for your Mac. Copy them out of your own Terminal and run them. On an Apple Silicon Mac they look like this:

echo 'eval "$(/opt/homebrew/bin/brew shellenv)"' >> ~/.zprofile
eval "$(/opt/homebrew/bin/brew shellenv)"

blocks.label: Intel Macs
blocks.text: On an Intel Mac, Homebrew installs to `/usr/local` instead of `/opt/homebrew`, so those two lines say `/usr/local/bin/brew` instead. This is why you copy the lines Homebrew printed for you rather than the ones printed here. Confirm it worked by running `brew --version` again -- it should now print a version number instead of `command not found`.
Now install the client. `libpq` is the PostgreSQL client package: it gives you `psql` without installing a database server on your Mac, which you do not need -- your server is Supabase.
brew install libpq

Homebrew installs `libpq` as keg-only, meaning it deliberately does not link it into your normal command folders (so it cannot collide with Apple's own copy or a full PostgreSQL install). `PATH` is the list of folders your shell searches for commands, so you add libpq's folder to it yourself. The line below appends one line to `~/.zshrc`, your shell's configuration file, then reloads it. `brew --prefix libpq` works out the right folder on both Intel and Apple Silicon, so you do not have to know which Mac you own.

echo 'export PATH="'$(brew --prefix libpq)'/bin:$PATH"' >> ~/.zshrc
source ~/.zshrc
psql --version
That last line is the proof: you should now see `psql (PostgreSQL) 17.x` or similar. If you still get `command not found`, close the Terminal window, open a new one, and try `psql --version` again.

blocks.label: If your shell is not zsh
blocks.text: macOS has used zsh by default since Catalina, so `~/.zshrc` and `~/.zprofile` are almost certainly right. Check with `echo $SHELL`. If it prints something ending in `/bash`, use `~/.bash_profile` everywhere these instructions say `~/.zshrc` or `~/.zprofile`.

Now connect. Wrap the connection string in single quotes, and leave the password out of the command -- psql will prompt you for it, which keeps your password out of your shell history file. Replace the user and host with your own.
psql 'postgresql://postgres.[PROJECT-REF]@aws-N-[REGION].pooler.supabase.com:5432/postgres'

psql prints `Password for user postgres.[PROJECT-REF]:`. Type or paste your password and press `Return` -- nothing appears on screen while you type, which is deliberate. A successful connection changes your prompt to `postgres=>` (some setups show `postgres=#`).

blocks.label: Single quotes, not double
blocks.text: If you do put the password inline, use single quotes: `psql 'postgresql://...'`. Double quotes still let zsh expand `$`, backticks, and backslashes inside the string, so a password containing `$` would be silently mangled into something else and you would get an authentication failure you cannot explain. Single quotes protect everything except a single-quote character.
Prove you are talking to the right database. Run these two lines, pressing `Return` after each:

SELECT current_database(), current_user;
\dt

`SELECT current_database(), current_user;` is ordinary SQL and must end in a semicolon; it should report the database `postgres`. `\dt` is a psql meta-command (not SQL, no semicolon) that lists the tables in your search path -- that is the `public` schema -- so you should see your KimTay tables. If it prints `Did not find any relations.` you are connected to an empty project, not the one holding your course data. To run a script you have saved, quit and use the `-f` flag:
psql 'postgresql://postgres.[PROJECT-REF]@aws-N-[REGION].pooler.supabase.com:5432/postgres' -f ~/Desktop/my-queries.sql
When you are done, leave psql with `\q`, which returns you to the normal Terminal prompt:
\q

blocks.label: Percent-encoding
blocks.text: A connection string is a URL, so the characters `@`, `:`, `/`, `#`, and `?` already mean something structural in it. If your database password contains any of them and you paste it inline, the string is parsed wrongly and the connection fails. You can percent-encode them by hand (`@` becomes `%40`, `#` becomes `%23`), but it is easier to let psql prompt you for the password as shown above, or to reset the password at `Database` then `Settings` to something using only letters and digits.

blocks.label: You are connecting as an owner, so RLS does not apply
blocks.text: Both routes log you in as the `postgres` role, which owns your tables. In PostgreSQL a table's owner is not subject to that table's Row Level Security policies unless the table was explicitly set to `FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY`. So a query that returns rows here may return nothing through Supabase's API, where requests run as a restricted role. That is expected, not a bug. Worth knowing for later: tables you create with the Supabase Table Editor get RLS switched on for you, while tables you create by running `CREATE TABLE` in the SQL editor do not.
When it does not work

blocks.caption: The errors Mac students actually hit
rows: `zsh: command not found: psql`
`psql` is installed but not on your `PATH`, or `libpq` never installed.
Re-run the `echo ... >> ~/.zshrc` and `source ~/.zshrc` lines, or just open a new Terminal window. Confirm the package is there with `brew list libpq`.
`FATAL: password authentication failed for user ...`
The password is wrong, or you left the literal `[YOUR-PASSWORD]` placeholder in the string, or a `$` in your password was expanded by double quotes.

Reset the password at `Database` then `Settings`, choosing letters and digits only. Copy the string again and replace the whole placeholder, brackets included -- or omit the password and let psql prompt you.
`Tenant or user not found`
The user name lost its project reference. This message comes from the pooler, not from PostgreSQL.
The user must read `postgres.` followed by your project reference, not plain `postgres`. Re-copy it from the `Connect` panel.
`Connection timed out`, or the client hangs with no message at all
You used the direct connection, which is IPv6-only on the free plan, and your network is IPv4.
Go back to `Connect` and copy the `Session pooler` string instead. Confirm the host ends in `pooler.supabase.com` and the port is `5432`.
`could not translate host name ... to address` or `nodename nor servname provided`
The host name is wrong -- usually a typo, a truncated paste, or a host copied from a tutorial with the wrong `aws-N` prefix or region.
Re-copy the host from your own `Connect` panel with the copy icon. Do not retype it by hand.
`server does not support SSL, but SSL was required`
Rare against Supabase. It means the client is demanding a stricter SSL mode than it can verify -- for example `verify-full` with no root certificate loaded.

Set `SSL mode` to `require` (pgAdmin: `Parameters` tab, `+`, `SSL mode`). `prefer` also works and is the default in both apps. Supabase does not force SSL by default, so plain `prefer` will connect and still encrypts.

items: You copied a `Session pooler` connection string from the `Connect` button, using your own project's host, not one typed from an example.
The user in your connection includes the dot and your project reference, and the password replaced the whole `[YOUR-PASSWORD]` placeholder, brackets and all.
Either TablePlus or pgAdmin 4 connects and lists your KimTay tables under the `public` schema, or `psql` gives you a `postgres=>` prompt.
`SELECT current_database(), current_user;` runs without error and reports the database `postgres`.
`\dt` in psql, or the table list in your GUI, shows the KimTay tables -- not `Did not find any relations.`
You saved the connection in your client, or saved the connection string in a file you can find, so you do not have to redo any of this next week.
You know how to reset the database password at `Database` then `Settings` if you ever lose it.

title: Connect from your own machine: Windows

blocks.text: By the end of this section you will have your Supabase database open on your own Windows machine in two different ways: in `pgAdmin 4`, a point-and-click tool with a tree of tables you can browse, and in `psql`, the command-line client, run from PowerShell. Both talk to the same database you created in the browser, so a table you build here shows up in the Supabase `Table Editor` a second later. You do not need a local PostgreSQL server for any of this. You only need the client tools and your connection string.

blocks.label: Before you start
blocks.text: You need three things: a Supabase project you already created, the database password you chose when you created it, and a Windows 10 or Windows 11 machine where you are allowed to install software. Budget about 20 minutes. On a school lab machine without administrator rights you can still install `pgAdmin 4` for the current user, and you can still edit your own `User variables` `Path`, but you cannot edit `System variables` -- the steps below say where that matters. If you cannot install anything at all, everything in this section can also be done in the Supabase `SQL Editor` in the browser.
Step 1: copy your connection string

Every tool below asks for the same five facts: host, port, database name, user, and password. Supabase hands you all five in one line of text called a connection string. It lives behind the `Connect` button at the top of your project dashboard. Older tutorials send you digging through `Project Settings`; the `Connect` button is the current path and it is faster.

items.title: Open your project
items.body: Go to `supabase.com/dashboard` and click your project. Free projects are paused after about a week with no database activity. If yours says `Paused`, click `Restore project` and wait for the dashboard to finish loading before continuing. You will know it worked when the project overview page shows charts instead of a paused banner.

items.title: Click Connect
items.body: The `Connect` button sits at the top of the dashboard, near the project name. A panel opens listing several connection strings, each with its own tab or heading.

items.title: Choose the session-mode pooler on port 5432
items.body: Pick the string labelled `Session pooler`. Some dashboards now label this group `Shared pooler` with a `Session mode` choice -- it is the same thing. Whatever the label, the string you want has `pooler.supabase.com` in the host and ends with `:5432/postgres`. Do not take the `:6543` string: that is transaction mode, which drops session features such as prepared statements and will make ordinary tools behave strangely. Do not take `Direct connection` either: that host (`db.<ref>.supabase.co`) resolves only to an IPv6 address unless the project has the paid IPv4 add-on, and most home and campus networks in the United States are still IPv4-only, so it looks like it hangs and then times out. The shared pooler answers on IPv4 on every plan, including Free.

items.title: Copy it and paste your password in
items.body: The copied string contains the placeholder `[YOUR-PASSWORD]`, brackets included. Replace that whole placeholder, brackets and all, with the database password you chose when you created the project. Nothing else in the string changes.

items.title: Park it somewhere safe for the next twenty minutes
items.body: Paste it into Notepad while you work through this section. Do not paste it into a shared document, a Discord channel, or a GitHub repository -- it is the key to your database.

blocks.text: postgresql://postgres.abcdefghijklmnopqrst:MyDbPassw0rd@aws-1-us-east-1.pooler.supabase.com:5432/postgres

That is an example, not your string. Copy yours from the `Connect` panel and never retype this one: the host prefix is `aws-0` on some projects and `aws-1` on others, and the region part changes with where your project lives. The panel may also start the string with `postgres://` instead of `postgresql://`; both are accepted, so leave whichever you were given.

Read your line left to right and you have every field the tools ask for: the user is `postgres.abcdefghijklmnopqrst` (the word `postgres`, a dot, then your project reference), the password comes after the colon, the host is everything between `@` and the last colon, the port is `5432`, and the database name after the final slash is `postgres`.

blocks.label: If your password contains punctuation
blocks.text: A connection string is a URL, so a few characters cannot appear in the password as-is: `@`, `:`, `/`, `?`, `#`, `[`, `]` and `%`. If your password contains any of them, replace each one with its percent code inside the string -- `@` becomes `%40`, `#` becomes `%23`, `?` becomes `%3F`, `/` becomes `%2F`, `:` becomes `%3A`, `%` becomes `%25`. So `p@ss#1` is written `p%40ss%231`. Supabase does not do this escaping for you when it builds the string, which is why a correct password can still produce a confusing failure. The `-h -p -d -U` flag form shown later avoids the problem entirely, because there the password is typed at a prompt rather than embedded in a URL.

blocks.label: Lost the password
blocks.text: The database password is shown once, when the project is created. Supabase cannot show it to you again. If you do not have it, set a new one from the dashboard: `Database` in the left sidebar, then `Settings` (the page whose address ends in `/database/settings`), then `Reset database password`. In older dashboards the same page is `Project Settings` then `Database`. Resetting briefly restarts the database and breaks every tool you already saved the old password in, so update `pgAdmin` afterwards and copy a fresh connection string.
Step 2: connect with pgAdmin 4

`pgAdmin 4` is the free, official graphical client for PostgreSQL. If you install PostgreSQL from the EDB installer described in step 3, `pgAdmin 4` comes bundled with it and there is nothing else to download. If you would rather not install a server at all, download `pgAdmin 4` on its own from `pgadmin.org/download/pgadmin-4-windows/` -- the current release is version 9.x, the installer is digitally signed, and it supports Windows 10 and later. Either way, launch it from the Start menu by typing `pgAdmin`. The first launch takes a few seconds and opens in a window that looks like a web page; that is normal.

items.title: Set a master password if you are asked for one
items.body: Some installs ask you to create a `master password` on first launch. This is a local password that protects the saved server passwords on this computer; it is not your Supabase password. Since version 7.2, pgAdmin uses the Windows credential store when it can and may never ask, so do not go looking for the prompt if it does not appear. If you do get it, pick something you will remember and write it down.

items.title: Register the server
items.body: In the left panel (the `Object Explorer`), right-click `Servers` and choose `Register` then `Server...`. In some builds this reads `Create` then `Server...`. A dialog opens with tabs across the top: `General`, `Connection`, `Parameters`, and a few more.

items.title: General tab
items.body: In `Name`, type something you will recognise, for example `Supabase KimTay`. This name is only a label for you and has no effect on the connection.

items.title: Connection tab
items.body: Fill in `Host name/address`, `Port`, `Maintenance database`, `Username`, and `Password` from your connection string, using the table below. Type the password in plainly here -- do not percent-encode it in pgAdmin, because this is not a URL. Tick `Save password?` so you are not retyping it every session.

items.title: Parameters tab
items.body: Click `+` to add a parameter, choose `SSL mode`, and set it to `require`. pgAdmin's default is `prefer`, which already encrypts the connection to Supabase, so this is a belt-and-braces step rather than a requirement; `require` makes it an error rather than a silent fallback if encryption is ever unavailable. In older builds this setting sits on a tab named `SSL` instead.

items.title: Save and check
items.body: Click `Save`. You will know it worked when the server appears in the tree with a coloured (not greyed-out) icon and no error dialog. Expand `Supabase KimTay` then `Databases` then `postgres` then `Schemas` then `public` then `Tables` to see the tables you have created. If you have not created any yet, `Tables` expands to nothing -- that is expected, not a failure.

blocks.label: Running SQL in pgAdmin
blocks.text: With your database selected in the tree, open `Tools` then `Query Tool`. That gives you an editor exactly like the Supabase `SQL Editor`. Paste your `CREATE TABLE REP ...` statement and press `F5` to run it; the `Data Output` panel at the bottom reports how long it took, and `Messages` shows `CREATE TABLE` when it succeeded. `Tools` also has a `PSQL Tool`, which is a real `psql` session embedded in pgAdmin -- a useful fallback if step 3 gives you trouble, since it needs no PATH setup.

`TablePlus` is a popular alternative with a cleaner interface, and it runs on Windows. It is paid software with a trial that has no published expiry date, but the trial limits you to two open tabs and two open windows at a time, and advanced filters are not available in the free version on Windows at all. Licences start at $99 one time for a single device. For this course `pgAdmin 4` does everything you need at no cost, so treat `TablePlus` as optional.
Step 3: get psql and run it from PowerShell

`psql` is the text client that ships with PostgreSQL. It is worth learning because every server, every tutorial, and every job posting assumes it. On Windows the usual way to get it is the EDB installer that `postgresql.org` links to, and you can install the client tools without installing a database server on your laptop.

items.title: Download the installer
items.body: Go to `enterprisedb.com/downloads/postgres-postgresql-downloads` and download the `Windows x86-64` installer for the newest version listed (18.4 at the time of writing). This is the download that `postgresql.org/download/windows/` links to. There is no 32-bit build any more.

items.title: Run it and reach Select Components
items.body: Right-click the downloaded file and choose `Run as administrator` if you have that right; otherwise just run it. Accept the default install directory. On the `Select Components` screen you will see four checkboxes: `PostgreSQL Server`, `pgAdmin 4`, `Stack Builder`, and `Command Line Tools`.

items.title: Choose what to install
items.body: `Command Line Tools` is the component that provides `psql` -- leave it checked. Leave `pgAdmin 4` checked so you get the graphical client from step 2 for free. You can uncheck `PostgreSQL Server` and `Stack Builder`, because your database lives at Supabase, not on your laptop. If you do leave the server checked, the installer will ask you to set a local superuser password and a port; that password has nothing to do with Supabase, and you can ignore the local server afterwards.

items.title: Note the install folder
items.body: The tools land in `C:\Program Files\PostgreSQL\18\bin`, where `18` is the major version you installed -- open `C:\Program Files\PostgreSQL` in File Explorer and use whatever number you actually see there. Go into `bin` and confirm `psql.exe` is present. Leave the File Explorer address bar showing that full path; you are about to copy it.

items.title: Add that folder to PATH
items.body: The installer does not put this folder on the system path, so Windows does not yet know where `psql.exe` is. Press the Windows key, type `environment`, and open `Edit the system environment variables`. In `System Properties` click `Environment Variables...`. If you have administrator rights, select `Path` under `System variables`; if you do not, select `Path` under `User variables for <your name>` instead -- either works for your own account. Click `Edit`, click `New`, paste `C:\Program Files\PostgreSQL\18\bin` (with your version number), then click `OK` on all three dialogs. There must be no quotation marks and no trailing backslash.

items.title: Open a fresh PowerShell and verify
items.body: Close every PowerShell and Command Prompt window you already had open -- they captured the old PATH and will not see the change. Open a new one from the Start menu (type `powershell`) and run the two checks below.

blocks.text:
where.exe psql
psql --version

`where.exe psql` should print the full path to `psql.exe`; it is how you prove the PATH edit took effect. Use `where.exe`, with the extension, because a bare `where` in PowerShell means something else entirely. Then `psql --version` should print a line like `psql (PostgreSQL) 18.4`. If the version printed is older than the one you installed, some other copy of `psql` is earlier in your PATH -- the path from `where.exe` tells you which.

Now connect. Wrap the connection string in single quotation marks. Unquoted, PowerShell treats several characters that can appear in a password as punctuation of its own: `&` is reserved and produces `The ampersand (&) character is not allowed`, `;` ends the command, `#` starts a comment, and a space splits the argument in two. Single quotes rather than double quotes matter, because inside double quotes PowerShell expands anything starting with `$`, so a password containing `$` would silently arrive wrong. If your password itself contains a single quote, double it (`''`) inside the quoted string.
psql 'postgresql://postgres.abcdefghijklmnopqrst:MyDbPassw0rd@aws-1-us-east-1.pooler.supabase.com:5432/postgres'

When it connects, PowerShell prints a `psql` banner and the prompt changes to `postgres=>`. That prompt is how you know you are in. From there you are typing SQL, and every statement ends with a semicolon -- until you type the semicolon and press Enter, `psql` keeps waiting and shows a `postgres->` continuation prompt instead. A few commands start with a backslash; those are `psql`'s own shortcuts, not SQL, and they do not take a semicolon.

\dt
SELECT REP_NUM, LAST_NAME, FIRST_NAME FROM REP;
\d CUSTOMER
\q

`\dt` lists your tables, `\d CUSTOMER` describes one table the way `DESCRIBE` does in MySQL, and `\q` quits back to PowerShell. Two things will surprise you. First, `\dt` prints your table names in lower case (`rep`, `customer`) even though you created them in capitals: PostgreSQL folds unquoted identifiers to lower case, and `psql` folds the name in `\d CUSTOMER` the same way, which is why the capitalised version still matches. Second, `\dt` and the `SELECT` only work once the tables exist -- if you have not run your `CREATE TABLE` statements yet, run them first, here or in the Supabase `SQL Editor`.

blocks.label: Keep your password out of your history
blocks.text: PowerShell records every command you type in `%APPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\PSReadLine\ConsoleHost_history.txt`, so the line above leaves your password in a plain text file that survives reboots. On a lab or shared machine, pass the pieces as flags instead and let `psql` prompt you: `psql -h aws-1-us-east-1.pooler.supabase.com -p 5432 -d postgres -U postgres.abcdefghijklmnopqrst`. This form also sidesteps percent-encoding, since the password is never part of a URL. Nothing appears on screen while you type the password, not even dots. That is normal -- type it and press Enter.

blocks.label: If you would rather not touch PATH
blocks.text: You can run `psql` by its full path without editing any environment variable. In PowerShell a quoted path has to be launched with the call operator `&`: `& 'C:\Program Files\PostgreSQL\18\bin\psql.exe' 'postgresql://...'`. The `PSQL Tool` inside pgAdmin (`Tools` then `PSQL Tool`) is another PATH-free way to get the same prompt.
When it does not work

blocks.caption: Windows connection problems and what to do about them
rows: `'psql' is not recognized as the name of a cmdlet`
Windows cannot find `psql.exe`

The PATH entry is missing, mistyped, or the window is stale. Run `where.exe psql` -- if it prints nothing, re-check the `Path` entry (no quotes, no trailing backslash, correct version number), then close every PowerShell window and open a new one.
`psql: error: connection to server ... FATAL: Tenant or user not found`
The pooler did not recognise the user name
On the pooler the user must be `postgres.` plus your project reference, not plain `postgres`. Re-copy the whole string from the `Connect` panel rather than editing the old one by hand.
The password prompt repeats, or `password authentication failed for user`
Wrong password, or punctuation in the password broke the URL

Re-check the password. If it contains `@ : / ? # [ ] %`, percent-encode those characters inside the connection string, or switch to the `-h -p -d -U` flag form and type the password at the prompt. If the password is genuinely lost, reset it at `Database` then `Settings` and copy a fresh string.
`The ampersand (&) character is not allowed`
PowerShell is reading part of your connection string as a command
Wrap the whole string in single quotation marks, or use the `-h -p -d -U` flag form instead.
You connect but the password is rejected only in PowerShell, never in pgAdmin
Your password contains `$` and you used double quotes
PowerShell expanded it as a variable. Use single quotes.
`could not connect to server: Connection timed out` after a long wait
You are on the direct connection (`db.` host) and your network is IPv4-only, or a firewall blocks outbound port 5432

Use the session-mode pooler string with the `pooler.supabase.com` host. If that still times out, test on a phone hotspot to confirm the school network is the blocker, and use the Supabase `SQL Editor` in the browser meanwhile.
pgAdmin: `could not translate host name ... to address`
A typo in the host, or the square brackets were left in
Retype the host from the `Connect` panel. There should be no `[` or `]` anywhere in any field, and the prefix is `aws-0` or `aws-1` depending on the project -- do not copy the example from this page.
An SSL or certificate error in pgAdmin
The `SSL mode` parameter is set to something stricter than your setup supports
Set `SSL mode` to `require` on the `Parameters` tab. `verify-full` additionally needs the Supabase CA certificate downloaded from `Database` then `Settings`; you do not need it for this course.
You connect, but `\dt` says `Did not find any relations`
You are connected to an empty schema
That is expected until you run your `CREATE TABLE` statements. Run them here or in the Supabase `SQL Editor`, then try `\dt` again. Remember the names come back in lower case.

blocks.label: Windows Defender Firewall
blocks.text: Windows may pop up a firewall prompt the first time `pgAdmin` or `psql` runs. These tools make outbound connections only, so you can decline the prompt asking to allow incoming connections and everything will still work. If your school network blocks outbound port 5432 entirely, no local setting will fix that -- use the browser `SQL Editor` on campus and your own network at home.

blocks.label: Tables you create here are not protected by Row Level Security
blocks.text: Supabase turns on Row Level Security automatically for tables made in the `Table Editor`, but not for tables created with SQL -- which is what you are doing in `psql` and in the `Query Tool`. Your new table will show up in the `Table Editor` flagged as unrestricted, meaning anyone holding your project's public API key could read it. That is acceptable for coursework data, but get in the habit now: run `ALTER TABLE REP ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;` on any table holding data you would not publish.

items: `where.exe psql` prints a path ending in `\bin\psql.exe` in a newly opened PowerShell window.
`psql --version` prints a version number that matches the version you installed.
`psql '<your connection string>'` reaches the `postgres=>` prompt.
`\dt` lists the tables you have created so far, in lower case, or reports none if you have not created any yet.
`pgAdmin 4` shows your server in the left tree with no error, and expands down to `Schemas` then `public` then `Tables`.
A table you create in `psql` appears in the Supabase `Table Editor` in the browser after a refresh.
Your password is stored somewhere private, not in a shared file, a repository, or a screenshot.
