title: Postgres vs. MySQL: what changes from Module 3

blocks.text: Module 3 taught you SQL in MySQL. Supabase gives you Postgres. This section is the translation sheet: by the end of it you will know exactly which lines from your Module 3 script you can paste into the Supabase SQL Editor unchanged, which four or five lines need a small edit, why one of those edits (quoting) causes almost every error a student hits in their first Postgres hour, and how to read the error message when it happens anyway.

blocks.label: Before you start
blocks.text: You need two things open: your Module 3 `.sql` script (the one with `CREATE DATABASE`, `CREATE TABLE`, and the KimTay `INSERT` statements), and your Supabase project dashboard from the earlier sections of this module. Everything in this section can be done in the browser. A terminal is optional and is only mentioned where it is genuinely optional -- it is never the only way to do something.

The important thing to understand first: MySQL and Postgres are two products that both speak SQL. The language is standardized, so the parts you spent Module 3 on -- `SELECT`, `WHERE`, `INSERT`, table design, keys -- are the same in both. What differs is a thin layer of housekeeping around the edges: how you get a database, how you look at a table, how you spell an auto-numbered column, what quotation marks mean, and one Supabase-specific security switch that MySQL has no equivalent for. That is the whole list. It is shorter than it feels.

blocks.caption: Module 3 (MySQL) to Supabase (Postgres): the whole difference list
rows: Create a database
`CREATE DATABASE KimTay;` then `USE KimTay;`
Already done -- your project is the database. Tables go in the `public` schema.
See a table's columns
`DESCRIBE REP;`
Click the table in the Table Editor, or run the `information_schema` query below. (`\d rep` if you have `psql`.)
List all tables
`SHOW TABLES;`
The Table Editor sidebar, or query `information_schema.tables`. (`\dt` if you have `psql`.)
Auto-numbered key
`ID INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY`
`id INT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY`
Quote a column or table name
backticks: `` `REP_NUM` ``
double quotes: `"REP_NUM"` -- but usually do not quote at all
Quote a piece of text
`'Kaiser'` worked, and so did `"Kaiser"` under MySQL's default settings
`'Kaiser'` only. Double quotes always mean a column or table name.
Return the first 5 rows
`SELECT * FROM REP LIMIT 5;`
Identical: `SELECT * FROM rep LIMIT 5;`
Skip rows then return some
`LIMIT 20, 10` **or** `LIMIT 10 OFFSET 20`
`LIMIT 10 OFFSET 20` only -- Postgres rejects the comma form
Column types used by KimTay
`CHAR`, `VARCHAR`, `DECIMAL`, `DATE`, `SMALLINT`
Same names, no edits needed (one small `CHAR` display quirk is noted below)
Let the outside world read the table
Not applicable -- MySQL has no built-in web API
Supabase exposes `public` over an auto-generated API, so you must turn on Row Level Security. See the warning below.

blocks.text: You do not create the database -- you already have one

In Module 3 the first line of your script was `CREATE DATABASE`. In Supabase, creating the project created the database, and the connection you set up earlier in this module already points at it. So delete the `CREATE DATABASE` and `USE` lines from your Module 3 script. Start straight at `CREATE TABLE`.

blocks.label: How to run a statement, and how to know it worked
blocks.text: In the Supabase dashboard, open **SQL Editor** in the left sidebar, paste your SQL into the editor pane, and click **Run** (or press Ctrl+Enter, Cmd+Enter on a Mac). A statement like `CREATE TABLE` returns no rows, so a successful run shows a green success message reading `Success. No rows returned`. That message is what "it worked" looks like -- it is not an error. A failed run shows a red panel with the Postgres error text; read the first line of it, then check the troubleshooting table at the end of this section. To see the table you just made, open **Table Editor** in the left sidebar; if a brand-new table is not listed yet, reload the page.

New tables land in a schema called `public`. A schema is a named folder for tables inside one database. Postgres uses schemas heavily; MySQL treats the word `SCHEMA` as a plain synonym for `DATABASE`, which is why the same idea was called a database in Module 3. You can leave everything in `public` for this course. If you want the KimTay tables kept apart from anything else you build later, you can make your own folder:

blocks.label: Stick with public
blocks.text: The Table Editor and the auto-generated API look at `public` by default. A table in a schema of your own will not appear in the Table Editor until you change the schema dropdown at the top of the table list, and it will not be reachable through the Supabase API at all until you add the schema under **Project Settings > API > Exposed schemas** and run a set of `GRANT` statements for the `anon`, `authenticated`, and `service_role` roles. That is real work for no benefit in this course. Use `public`.

blocks.label: Supabase-only step: turn on Row Level Security
blocks.text: This has no MySQL equivalent, and skipping it is the single most consequential mistake you can make here. Supabase publishes every table in the `public` schema through an auto-generated web API. A table you create with the **Table Editor** gets Row Level Security (RLS) switched on for you. A table you create by running `CREATE TABLE` in the **SQL Editor** -- which is what you are about to do with your Module 3 script -- does **not**. Until you enable RLS and write a policy, the dashboard flags the table as unrestricted, and depending on your project's settings its rows may be readable by anyone holding your project's public key. Run the statements below immediately after creating each table. Enabling RLS with no policy denies all API access, which is the safe starting point -- your own SQL Editor queries keep working, because they do not go through the API.

-- run this right after every CREATE TABLE in the SQL Editor
ALTER TABLE public.rep ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;

-- check it: rowsecurity should be true for every table you made
SELECT tablename, rowsecurity
FROM pg_tables
WHERE schemaname = 'public'
ORDER BY tablename;
Inspecting a table: DESCRIBE has two replacements
`DESCRIBE REP;` does not exist in Postgres. There are two replacements, and the browser one needs nothing installed.

The browser way: open **Table Editor** from the left sidebar and click `rep`. The columns, types, and NOT NULL settings are on screen. That is your `DESCRIBE`. If you would rather have a query you can paste into the SQL Editor, this one works on any Postgres anywhere:

SELECT column_name, data_type, is_nullable
FROM information_schema.columns
WHERE table_schema = 'public'
  AND table_name   = 'rep'
ORDER BY ordinal_position;

blocks.label: Why table_schema is in that query
blocks.text: Without the `table_schema = 'public'` line, the query returns the columns of every table named `rep` in every schema you can see, so you would get each column listed more than once as soon as you had a second `rep` anywhere. Note also that both values are lowercase and in single quotes: `information_schema` stores identifiers as text, and Postgres stored your unquoted table name folded to lowercase. Searching for `'REP'` returns zero rows -- which is a confusing way to be told your table exists.

The terminal way, for reference: `psql` is the command-line Postgres client, and it has shortcuts called meta-commands. They begin with a backslash. They are `psql` features rather than SQL, so they take no semicolon, they are never sent to the server, and they will **not** work in the Supabase SQL Editor in the browser.

\dt          -- list tables on your current search path (public, by default)
\d rep       -- show columns, types, and keys for the rep table
\d+ rep      -- same, plus storage and description details

blocks.label: You do not need psql for this course
blocks.text: `psql` is not a separate download; it ships with a PostgreSQL installation, so getting it means installing Postgres locally even though your database lives in Supabase. If you want to try it, get the connection string from the **Connect** button at the top of your Supabase dashboard and use the **Session pooler** string, which Supabase recommends for `psql`. Everything this section asks you to do can be done in the browser instead, and nothing later in the course depends on `psql`.
Auto-numbering: AUTO_INCREMENT becomes IDENTITY

KimTay does not use auto-numbering -- `REP_NUM` and `CUSTOMER_NUM` are `CHAR` codes that the business assigns. But you will want it in your own tables, and `AUTO_INCREMENT` is a MySQL-only keyword that Postgres rejects with a syntax error. The modern, standard spelling is `GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY`. An identity column is automatically `NOT NULL`, so you do not add that yourself:

`ALWAYS` means Postgres owns the number: if you try `INSERT INTO note (note_id, body) VALUES (7, '...')` it refuses, which is exactly the accident you want blocked. (There is an escape hatch, `OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE`, for the rare times you need it.) If you want MySQL's more permissive behaviour, where supplying your own value is allowed and only a missing value is generated, write `GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY` instead.

You will also see `SERIAL` in older tutorials (`note_id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY`). It still works and produces a similar auto-numbered column, but it is a Postgres-specific shorthand that creates a separate sequence object and lets anyone insert their own value. `GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY` is the one to learn: it is the SQL standard, and it is what current Postgres documentation steers you toward.
Quoting: the difference that causes the most confusion

In MySQL, backticks protect a name and everything keeps the case you typed. Postgres has a different rule, and it is worth reading twice: an identifier that is not quoted is folded to lowercase. `REP_NUM`, `Rep_Num`, and `rep_num` all become `rep_num`. An identifier that is wrapped in double quotes keeps its case exactly and must be double-quoted every single time you mention it afterwards. (Postgres folds down; the SQL standard actually says to fold up. Nobody agrees, which is the real reason the safe advice is to never quote and always type lowercase.)

blocks.label: The case-folding trap
blocks.text: If you create a table as `CREATE TABLE "REP" ("REP_NUM" CHAR(2));` then `SELECT * FROM REP;` fails with `relation "rep" does not exist` -- Postgres folded your query to lowercase, but the table is genuinely named uppercase `REP`. From then on you must write `SELECT "REP_NUM" FROM "REP";` forever. Fix: never put double quotes around table or column names when you create them. Type them unquoted, in lowercase, and Postgres will let you refer to them in any case you like. If you have already done it, the repair is `ALTER TABLE "REP" RENAME TO rep;` -- and note you must quote the old name to say it, and must not quote the new one.

So when you port the Module 3 DDL, drop the backticks and do not replace them with double quotes. This is the safe version, and after it every one of `SELECT REP_NUM FROM REP;`, `SELECT rep_num FROM rep;` and `SELECT Rep_Num FROM Rep;` returns the same rows:

CREATE TABLE rep (
  rep_num    CHAR(2) PRIMARY KEY,
  last_name  VARCHAR(15) NOT NULL,
  first_name VARCHAR(15) NOT NULL,
  street     VARCHAR(20),
  city       VARCHAR(15),
  state      CHAR(2),
  zip        CHAR(5),
  commission DECIMAL(8,2),
  rate       DECIMAL(4,2)
);

ALTER TABLE public.rep ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;

blocks.label: Two kinds of quote
blocks.text: In Postgres, single quotes mean "this is a piece of text" and double quotes mean "this is the name of a table or column". They are not interchangeable. MySQL, under its default settings, let you write `"Kaiser"` as a string; Postgres reads that as a column named `Kaiser` and answers `column "Kaiser" does not exist`. Backticks are neither -- Postgres does not use them at all and reports a syntax error the moment it sees one.

blocks.label: Apostrophes inside text
blocks.text: This part did not change. To store a name like `O'Brien`, double the apostrophe: `'O''Brien'`. Those are two single quotes in a row, not one double quote. It works the same way in MySQL and Postgres.
Data types: most of them carry over untouched

Every type in the KimTay schema exists in Postgres under the same name: `CHAR(2)`, `VARCHAR(35)`, `DECIMAL(9,2)`, `DATE`, and `SMALLINT`. You can copy those column definitions across with no edits at all. `DECIMAL` is simply another name for Postgres's `NUMERIC`, so your money columns keep their exactness. `SMALLINT` holds -32768 to 32767, the same range you learned. Dates still go in as `'2026-09-14'`, year first -- that year-first ISO form is the one Postgres documents as unambiguous.

blocks.caption: MySQL types that need a different name in Postgres
rows: `INT AUTO_INCREMENT`
`INT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY`
`AUTO_INCREMENT` is a MySQL-only keyword; Postgres reports a syntax error
`DATETIME`
`TIMESTAMP`, or better `TIMESTAMPTZ`
There is no `datetime` type in Postgres. `TIMESTAMPTZ` (short for `timestamp with time zone`) is the Supabase default and the safer choice for real events. `DATE` is unchanged.
`TINYINT(1)` for yes/no
`BOOLEAN` with `TRUE` / `FALSE`
Postgres has a real boolean type
`DOUBLE`
`DOUBLE PRECISION`
Postgres does not accept bare `DOUBLE`. Naming only -- but keep money in `DECIMAL`, which the Postgres docs recommend for exact amounts.

blocks.label: One CHAR quirk worth knowing
blocks.text: `CHAR(n)` pads short values with spaces in both products, but they hand the value back differently: MySQL strips the trailing spaces when you read the column, while Postgres stores and displays them. For KimTay this changes nothing you can see, because `rep_num` is exactly 2 characters and `zip` is exactly 5, so there is no padding. It matters the day you put `'Kaiser'` in a `CHAR(20)`: Postgres returns it with fourteen trailing spaces. If that ever bites you, use `VARCHAR` -- which is what the Postgres documentation recommends for most columns anyway.
What does not change

Almost everything. `SELECT`, `FROM`, `WHERE`, `AND`, `OR`, `NOT`, `IN`, `BETWEEN`, `LIKE`, `IS NULL`, `ORDER BY`, `GROUP BY`, `HAVING`, `COUNT`, `SUM`, `AVG`, `MIN`, `MAX`, joins, `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`, `PRIMARY KEY`, `FOREIGN KEY`, `NOT NULL`, `DEFAULT` -- identical, character for character. `LIMIT 5` behaves the same in both. `NULL` still means "no value recorded" and still refuses to equal anything, so you still test it with `IS NULL` rather than `= NULL`.

Everything from Module 2 carries over completely, because none of it was ever about a particular product. Functional dependence, candidate keys, primary keys, foreign keys, first, second, and third normal form, ER diagrams -- those are properties of the relational model itself. A design that is in 3NF in MySQL is in 3NF in Postgres. The reason Module 2 came before Module 3 is exactly this: the thinking outlasts the tool.
When it goes wrong: the five errors you will actually see
Postgres error messages are blunt but honest. Read the first line, find it here, apply the fix, and re-run. Nothing in this table requires starting over.

title: Keeping your database safe

blocks.text: Your project now holds real data on a real server on the internet, which means it has secrets attached to it. This section gets you to the point where you can name every secret Supabase gave you, say out loud which one is allowed to appear in code other people can read, fix a password you accidentally pasted somewhere public, and keep a copy of your own work that survives anything that happens to the project. None of this takes long, and doing it once now saves you a bad afternoon later.
You were given three different secrets, and they do not do the same job

People new to this tend to treat every long random string as one thing called "the key". Supabase hands you three, and the difference between them is the difference between a safe project and a project anyone can empty. Here is what each one is for.

blocks.caption: The three credentials on a Supabase project
headers: May it appear in code a user can see?
rows: Database password
The password for the Postgres `postgres` user -- it is the part you paste into the connection string you use in `psql`, pgAdmin, or TablePlus.
No. It belongs in your connection tool and nowhere else.
Publishable key (starts with `sb_publishable_`; older docs and older projects call this the `anon` key)
A public, low-privilege key that identifies your project to the outside world. What it is allowed to read or change is decided by Row Level Security.
Yes. This is the only one designed to be shipped in a browser app.
Secret key (starts with `sb_secret_`; older docs and older projects call this the `service_role` key)
A key that bypasses Row Level Security completely and can read, change, or delete every row in every table.
Never. Not in a browser app, not in a public repository, not in a screenshot.

blocks.label: Two naming systems, same two jobs
blocks.text: Supabase is in the middle of renaming its API keys. Projects created recently show `sb_publishable_...` and `sb_secret_...`. Older projects and most tutorials show `anon` and `service_role`, which are JSON Web Tokens (long strings with two dots in them). Both systems work today, and Supabase has said the legacy `anon` and `service_role` keys will be deprecated by the end of 2026. Whichever pair your project shows, the rule is identical: the low-privilege one (publishable / `anon`) is public, the high-privilege one (secret / `service_role`) is not.
These three things live in three different places, and this trips people up:

items: **Connection strings** come from the `Connect` button at the top of your project dashboard. Note that the string it gives you has `[YOUR-PASSWORD]` in it as a placeholder -- Supabase does not put your real password there.

**API keys** (publishable and secret, or `anon` and `service_role`) are under `Settings` -> `API Keys`. Newer projects split them across a `Publishable and secret API keys` tab and a `Legacy API keys` tab. The publishable key also appears inside the `Connect` dialog's framework code snippets.

**The database password** is not displayed anywhere, ever. Supabase shows it to you once when you create the project and never again. If you do not have it written down, your only option is to reset it, which you do at `Database` -> `Settings`.

blocks.label: If a tutorial sends you somewhere that does not exist
blocks.text: Older tutorials tell you to look under `Project Settings` -> `Database` for a connection string. Supabase reorganized the dashboard, so connection strings now come from the `Connect` button and password resets live at `Database` -> `Settings`. If a tutorial's menu path does not match what you see on screen, the tutorial is out of date, not your project.

blocks.label: The secret key is the whole database
blocks.text: Treat the secret key (`sb_secret_...`, or `service_role` on an older project) exactly the way you would treat your own bank login. It ignores every security rule you set up, so anyone holding it can read your `CUSTOMER` table, empty your `INVOICE` table, or drop your schema. It is meant only for code running on a server you control, read from an environment variable that is not committed. If you paste it into front-end JavaScript, into a public GitHub repo, or into a Discord message asking for help, assume it is compromised. Go to `Settings` -> `API Keys` and revoke or rotate it right away -- for legacy `service_role` keys this is the `Legacy API keys` tab; for new-style keys you can revoke the one key that leaked and create a replacement.
Row Level Security, in one sentence

blocks.label: Row Level Security (RLS)
blocks.text: Row Level Security is a Postgres feature that decides, row by row, whether the person asking is allowed to see or change that row -- so two users hitting the same `SELECT` can get different results.

Two things surprise students here. First, whether RLS is on depends on how you made the table: tables created through the dashboard `Table Editor` get RLS enabled for you, while tables you create by running `CREATE TABLE` in the `SQL Editor` do not. Second, RLS turned on with no policies written means nobody gets any rows through the public API -- that is the correct, safe default, not a bug.

That explains the classic confusion: you connect with `psql` using the database password, run `SELECT * FROM CUSTOMER;`, and see all four customers -- but a web page using the publishable key shows an empty list. Two separate reasons let `psql` through. You are connected as the `postgres` role, which owns those tables, and Postgres exempts a table's owner from that table's RLS policies unless the table was explicitly set to `FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY`. On top of that, the `postgres` role on Supabase carries the `BYPASSRLS` attribute. The web page has neither: it arrives as the low-privilege public role, and there is no policy telling Postgres to let it through.

blocks.label: Good enough for coursework, not for anything real
blocks.text: For this course you are the only person touching the KimTay tables, you are reaching them over `psql` or the `SQL Editor`, and nothing is exposed to the public. Leaving RLS off on your assignment tables is fine. The moment a table holds someone else's information, or a browser app can reach it with the publishable key, RLS off means anyone on the internet can read and rewrite that table. The difference is not the software -- it is who else can reach it.
If a password leaks, rotate it

Leaking happens in ordinary ways: you paste a connection string into a class chat to ask why it fails, you commit a `.env` file, you screen-share your terminal. There is no undo for a leaked secret -- the only real fix is to replace it so the old one stops working.

items.title: Open the database settings
items.body: In your project, go to `Database` -> `Settings` in the left sidebar. This is where the database password lives, separately from the `Connect` panel where you copy connection strings.

items.title: Reset the password
items.body: Find the `Database password` section and choose `Reset database password`. Let Supabase generate a strong one, then copy it into a password manager or a note before you close the dialog. You cannot read it back later -- if you lose it, your only move is to reset again. A generated password can contain characters like `@`, `#`, `/`, `:` or `?`, which is fine, but see the note below about what that means for connection strings.

items.title: Wait a minute, then rebuild your connection string
items.body: The reset can take a couple of minutes to take effect, so do not panic if the first attempt still fails. Then go back to `Connect` at the top of the dashboard, copy the session pooler string again, and replace the placeholder `[YOUR-PASSWORD]` with your new password. Delete the square brackets too -- leaving them in is the single most common reason this step fails. The old string is dead the moment the reset finishes.

items.title: Test the new string before you rely on it
items.body: Run `psql "YOUR-NEW-CONNECTION-STRING"` (quotes included) and then `SELECT 1;` at the `postgres=>` prompt. If you get back a table with a `1` in it, the string is good. Type `\q` to quit. If you get `password authentication failed`, re-read the previous step -- brackets, or an un-encoded special character, are almost always the cause.

items.title: Update every place that stored the old one
items.body: Saved connections in pgAdmin or TablePlus, any `.env` file, and any note on your machine. If a tool suddenly says authentication failed, this is why.

items.title: Clean up the leak itself
items.body: Delete the chat message, and if the secret went into a Git commit, remember that deleting the line in a later commit does not remove it from history -- anyone can still read the old commit. Rotating is what makes it harmless.

blocks.label: Special characters in a password must be percent-encoded
blocks.text: A connection string is a URI, and Postgres requires characters with special meaning in a URI to be percent-encoded inside it. If your generated password contains `@`, `:`, `/`, `?`, `#`, `%`, `&` or a space, you must replace it in the string: `@` becomes `%40`, `:` becomes `%3A`, `/` becomes `%2F`, `#` becomes `%23`, `%` becomes `%25`, and a space becomes `%20`. A password of `p@ss/word` goes into the string as `p%40ss%2Fword`. Symptom when you get this wrong: `password authentication failed` even though you pasted the right password, or a confusing `could not translate host name` error, because everything after an un-encoded `@` was read as a server address. If you would rather not deal with this, reset the password and pick your own using only letters, digits, `-` and `_`.

blocks.label: Keep passwords out of your shell history
blocks.text: When you type a full connection string on the command line, the whole thing -- password included -- gets written to a plain text history file. On a Mac with zsh that is `~/.zsh_history`; on bash it is `~/.bash_history`; in Windows PowerShell it is `%APPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\PSReadLine\ConsoleHost_history.txt`. Separately, anything you type at the `postgres=>` prompt inside `psql` is saved to `~/.psql_history`. Prefer saving the connection in pgAdmin or TablePlus, or storing the string in a file you do not commit, rather than retyping it in the terminal all day.

blocks.label: Stop Git from ever seeing your secrets
blocks.text:
If your project folder is a Git repository, create a file named `.gitignore` in the top of that folder with these three lines in it, before you create any file that holds a secret:

```
.env
*.env
secrets.txt
```

Git only ignores files it is not already tracking, so this has to happen first. To confirm it worked, run `git status` -- your `.env` file should not appear in the list. If it does appear, it is already tracked, and you need `git rm --cached .env` and then a commit.
Your real backup is a .sql file you own

A Supabase Free plan project is paused after 7 days of inactivity, and the Free plan allows only 2 active projects at a time. Supabase keeps your data while a project is paused and gives you up to 1 year to restore it from the dashboard, so this is not an emergency -- but you still do not want your only copy of a graded assignment sitting somewhere you do not control, behind a login that could be down the night before it is due. This is exactly what Module 3-9, "Saving SQL Commands", was preparing you for -- now you are doing it for a real reason.

Keep one plain text file, in your own notes folder, containing every `CREATE TABLE` and `INSERT` you ran, in the order you ran them. That file is your backup, your rebuild script, and your submission all at once.

-- kimtay-setup.sql
-- KimTay Pet Supplies -- rebuild from empty
-- Last run: 2026-08-02

CREATE TABLE REP (
    REP_NUM     CHAR(2)         PRIMARY KEY,
    LAST_NAME   VARCHAR(15)     NOT NULL,
    FIRST_NAME  VARCHAR(15)     NOT NULL,
    STREET      VARCHAR(20),
    CITY        VARCHAR(15),
    STATE       CHAR(2),
    ZIP         CHAR(5),
    COMMISSION  DECIMAL(8,2),
    RATE        DECIMAL(4,2)
);

-- No column list here, so the values must be in exactly the
-- same order as the columns above. If you ever reorder the
-- CREATE TABLE, this INSERT breaks silently or loudly.
INSERT INTO REP VALUES
    ('20','Kaiser','Valerie','624 Randall','Grove','FL','33321',20542.50,0.05);

-- ...then CUSTOMER, ITEM, INVOICE, INVOICE_LINE in that order,
-- because each one references the tables above it.

Order matters. A table with a `REFERENCES` clause cannot be created before the table it points at, so `REP` comes before `CUSTOMER`, and `INVOICE` and `ITEM` both come before `INVOICE_LINE`. Writing the file in run order is what makes it work on a fresh project.
Prove the backup is real by running it

A backup you have never restored is a guess. Test it against an empty database -- and it has to be empty, because `CREATE TABLE REP` on a project that already has a `REP` table stops with `relation "rep" already exists`. Do not test it against the project holding your graded work.

The easiest way: create a second project (the Free plan allows 2 active ones), wait the minute or two it takes to provision, open the `SQL Editor`, paste the whole file in, and press `Run`. If you already have 2 active projects, pause one you are not using from its dashboard first.

If you have `psql` installed, you can do the same from a terminal. Two things to get right: you must be in the folder that holds the file, and you must add `-v ON_ERROR_STOP=1`. By default `psql` prints an error and keeps going, so a broken script can scroll a failure off your screen and still finish looking successful. That flag makes it stop at the first error, which is the whole point of a test.

# 1. Move into the folder that holds the file.
#    On Mac/Linux, type `cd ` (with the space), then drag the
#    folder from Finder onto the terminal window and press Enter.
cd ~/Documents/database-course

# 2. Confirm the file is actually here before you run anything.
ls kimtay-setup.sql          # Mac/Linux
# dir kimtay-setup.sql       # Windows PowerShell

# 3. Run it. The quotes around the connection string are required.
psql "YOUR-SESSION-POOLER-CONNECTION-STRING" -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -f kimtay-setup.sql

How you know it worked: `psql` echoes one line per statement -- `CREATE TABLE` for each table, `INSERT 0 1` for each single-row insert -- and returns you to your normal shell prompt with no red `ERROR:` text. In the `SQL Editor`, a green success message and no error panel means the same thing. Either way, do not take the absence of an error as proof. Ask the database what it actually has:

blocks.label: Why your tables come back lowercase
blocks.text: That first query lists `customer`, `invoice`, `invoice_line`, `item`, `rep` -- all lowercase, even though you typed `CREATE TABLE REP`. Postgres folds unquoted identifiers to lowercase. Nothing is wrong, and `SELECT * FROM REP;` still works, because that name gets folded the same way. You would only need to care if you had wrapped a name in double quotes when you created it.

blocks.label: What must never go in that file
blocks.text: The `.sql` file holds SQL only. No password, no connection string, no keys. Then it is safe to email to yourself, drop in cloud storage, or commit to a repository -- which is the entire point of keeping the secrets somewhere else.

items: You can say which of the three secrets is safe in front-end code, and it is the publishable key (the `anon` key on an older project) -- not the database password, not the secret / `service_role` key.
Your secret / `service_role` key exists only in the Supabase dashboard, or in a server-side file you have never committed.

You know the three different locations: connection strings from `Connect`, API keys at `Settings` -> `API Keys`, password reset at `Database` -> `Settings` -- and that the password itself is never displayed anywhere.
Your database password is written down somewhere you will still have it next month, because Supabase will not show it to you again.
You can explain in one sentence why `psql` shows rows that a browser app using the publishable key does not.
RLS being off on your KimTay tables is a decision you made knowingly, not a default you never looked at.
A `kimtay-setup.sql` file with every `CREATE TABLE` and `INSERT`, in run order, is saved in your own notes.

You have run that file once against an empty database with `-v ON_ERROR_STOP=1` (or in a fresh project's `SQL Editor`) and then confirmed with a `COUNT(*)` that the rows are really there -- not just that nothing turned red.
No file you have shared, committed, or pasted into a chat contains a password or a connection string, and `git status` does not list your `.env`.

4. MOST IMPORTANT BUG — the verification step did not verify. `psql -f` does NOT stop on error by default; it prints the error, continues, and still exits 0. A student whose `CREATE TABLE CUSTOMER` failed would watch the rest of the file run and conclude "no error, genuine backup". Added `-v ON_ERROR_STOP=1` to the command (confirmed against postgresql.org/docs/current/app-psql.html) and added an explicit ask-the-database verification pass (`information_schema.tables` + `COUNT(*)`), since "it didn't error" is not evidence.

5. RLS bypass explanation was imprecise. "The psql connection is the database owner and bypasses RLS" conflates two separate mechanisms. Corrected to: Postgres exempts a table's owner from its own RLS policies unless `FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY` is set, AND the Supabase `postgres` role additionally carries `BYPASSRLS`. Both facts are load-bearing and either alone explains the behaviour.

6. Rewrote "RLS is off or on depending on how you made the table" (grammatically garbled) while keeping the verified claim: Table Editor enables RLS, raw `CREATE TABLE` in the SQL Editor does not.
